hints: Look closely at the dark-stained vascular bundles in the corners of this square stem. Notice each bundle has two zones, an outer zone of small cells and an inner zone of much larger open tubes.
Remember where xylem sits in a stem vascular bundle relative to phloem, and which tissue has the very wide, lignified vessel lumens for water transport.
walkthrough:
**Orientate yourself in the stem**

Look at the whole section first. You can see a large central pith of big parenchyma cells, a ring of vascular bundles, and an outer cortex and epidermis. This is a typical young dicot stem.

Focus on the four large bundles in the corners.

**Recall the bundle plan**

In a stem vascular bundle, the tissues are arranged with phloem to the outside and xylem to the inside.

Xylem is easy to spot because it contains metaxylem vessels. These are very large, round, empty-looking tubes with thick lignified walls for carrying water.

**Match the labels to the tissues**

Label C points right into the inner part of the corner bundle, where you see those large open vessel lumens. That is classic xylem.

Label B points to the outer, smaller-celled part of the same bundle. That is phloem. Labels A and D are outside the bundles in ground and support tissue.

options.A: This points to the cortex parenchyma between the epidermis and the vascular bundles, not a transport tissue.
options.B: This points to the outer part of the vascular bundle with small densely packed cells, which is the phloem.
options.C: This points to the inner part of the vascular bundle with large lignified vessels, which is the xylem for water transport.
options.D: This points to the outer corner tissue under the epidermis, which is collenchyma for support, not xylem.
